reference.source: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
clinicalPearls: Presents with chronic watery, non-bloody diarrhoea similar to collagenous colitis, often with urgency and nocturnal symptoms
Affects both sexes more equally than collagenous colitis, though still with a female predominance, and typically in middle-aged and older adults
Colonoscopy shows normal-appearing mucosa, so diagnosis is made only on biopsy histology
The defining feature is a marked increase in intraepithelial lymphocytes without the thickened subepithelial collagen band that characterises collagenous colitis
Strongly associated with coeliac disease, autoimmune thyroid disease and drugs such as non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, proton-pump inhibitors and certain other agents
Multiple biopsies from several colonic segments improve diagnostic yield because changes may be patchy
Budesonide for microscopic colitis is first-line, with withdrawal of implicated drugs an essential first step
reference.pathophysiology: Lymphocytic colitis is a subtype of microscopic colitis defined histologically by a raised intraepithelial lymphocyte count in the surface epithelium with associated chronic inflammation of the lamina propria, but crucially without the thickened subepithelial collagen band seen in collagenous colitis, and with an endoscopically normal mucosa. It is thought to result from a dysregulated mucosal immune response to luminal antigens, including drugs, in predisposed individuals, disturbing epithelial water and electrolyte transport and producing a secretory watery diarrhoea. It shares many clinical and immunological features with collagenous colitis and the two are considered ends of a spectrum.
additionalInvestigations: Colonoscopy with segmental biopsies despite normal mucosal appearance
Histological quantification of intraepithelial lymphocytes and assessment for a collagen band
Coeliac serology and duodenal biopsy if indicated
Stool studies to exclude infective causes
redFlags: Rectal bleeding, which is not typical and should prompt reconsideration of the diagnosis
Marked weight loss requiring exclusion of coeliac disease or malignancy
Dehydration and electrolyte disturbance from severe diarrhoea
Anaemia suggesting an alternative or coexisting diagnosis
reference.prognosis: The disease is benign with no increased colorectal cancer risk; many patients respond to treatment and some experience spontaneous remission, though relapses may occur and require further courses of treatment.
pitfalls: Assuming irritable bowel syndrome and not biopsying normal-looking colonic mucosa
Failing to distinguish it from collagenous colitis by looking for the collagen band
Overlooking coexisting coeliac disease as a cause of persistent symptoms
Not reviewing medications that can precipitate or maintain the colitis
